To tackle the data sparsity problem affecting session-based recommendation models that predict the next item users will choose, researchers combined self-supervised learning with co-training. They proposed an enhanced framework by leveraging a session-based graph to create informative, not artificially sparse, data for these models. This new approach exploits internal and external session connections to produce contrastive learning, thereby preserving genuine data for superior session-based recommendation performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate the success of this innovative method in achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmark datasets. Interestingly, the developers found that co-training can be effectively applied to session-based recommendation, an area where it had previously not been utilized. Furthermore, they identified that the graph session-based recommender outperformed older techniques by nearly always surpassing their performance. Finally, they took a detailed look at how well different components of their proposed method performed and found that the contrastive learning technique drove the best results when applied to this specific problem domain. As a result, they concluded that incorporating contrastive learning can significantly enhance the performance of current session-based recommendation methods. The resulting method was dubbed CST and represents an innovative enhancement to standard session-based recommendation models by leveraging a graph to create informative data for superior performance. The code for this innovative method can be accessed via https://github.com/yangyangyang/CST. Additionally, they demonstrated the methodology using a video that illustrates: (a) how sessions are created from a choice of time units, and (b) how co-training enhances the graph-based recommender by contrasting real with artificial data. The vectors in question are shown using the uMAP visualization tool to illustrate (c) how low-dimensional mapping contributes to the success of this novel method. The corresponding authors are Yang Yang, Yang Du, and Xu Yan. The researchers tested their novel method against multiple recent state-of-the-art techniques including GRU4RE, STOGAE, SGLM, and GraphFM. The novel method performed exceptionally well, achieving between 0.65 and 2.05 million percentage points improvement over these benchmark techniques. The most prominent areas of enhancement were seen against GRU4RE and STOGAE, where the novel method delivered a million-plus percentage points improvement. The boost in performance was particularly evident when using the recent MuProp method, and was largely attributed to the unique data creation technique utilized. The novel method performed exceptionally well on diverse datasets, and was largely due to the unique data creation technique and the combination of contrastive learning with co-training. The associated technical report can be accessed via arxiv.org

This research presents a novel method for generating LCD codes using group rings and a standard transformation that maps group ring components to a subring of $n \times n$ matrices, resulting in LCD codes that are also group codes due to being ideals in a group ring. Under specific conditions for the group ring element $v$, the proposed construction allows for the creation of non-trivial group LCD codes, with additional constraints enabling the development of reversible group LCD codes. A variety of binary group LCD codes are presented, including optimal and reversible group LCD codes with various parameters. Furthermore, it is demonstrated how the group ring approach can be extended to various mathematical structures, such as rings formed by the direct sum of fields and groups, leading to the formation of LCD codes within these structures. The proposed techniques are supported by numerical examples and potential applications are also considered. These developments contribute to the ongoing study of group ring theory and its coding theory implications. To facilitate code evaluation, the associated matrices for the constructed binary group LCD codes are publicly available online. A document containing the code matrices can be accessed via the following link: https://users.math.unipd.it/~pagani/matdidattica/group_lcd_codes/matfiles/group_lcd_codes.mat. This program enables researchers to access a user-friendly interface for studying group ring theory and its coding theory implications, with a focus on LCD codes. We examine differential forms on an algebraic compactification of the metric graph moduli space, derived by mapping invariant differential forms from the tropical Torelli map. It's known that these invariant forms give rise to the stable real cohomology of the general linear group, a finding by Borel. We compute period integrals by integrating such forms across graph metrics and find them to be always finite and expressible as generalised Feynman integrals. Our integrals have further application in identifying non-zero classes in homology groups of the graph space and in describing its cohomology ring structure. Specifically, we evaluate the period integrals for the metric completion of the moduli space of finite metric graphs and find them to be equal to the metrically complete extension of the classical Feynman integrals. Along the way, we establish a novel connection between invariant differential forms and the metric graph space and obtain a novel realisation of the cohomology group as a class containing metrically complete stable forms. As a result, we obtain a novel expression for the Fefferman metric of the graph moduli space. Furthermore, we describe how the form algebra is linked to the metric graph's subcomplex moduli spaces, leading to an interesting homological and cohomological feature - that the homotopy groups of the graph space are capable of exhibiting non-zero values. Finally, the period integrals' property of being expressible as the stable forms' invariant combinations enables us to arrive at an interesting relationship between the graph space's cohomology and the homology groups of the general linear group. To conclude, we provide concrete examples which showcase the diverse range of topological properties that the graph space can exhibit. Additionally, we suggest several open challenges and conjectures related to the graph space's topology. The period integrals' relationship to the general linear group's cohomology also raises questions, waiting to be explored, about the topology of the graph space and its connection to the homology groups of the general linear group. The relationship between the graph space's cohomology and the homology groups of the general linear group can also be further studied by examining the stable forms' relationships with the linear group's Lie algebra and its Poisson structure. In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through linear diagnostic analysis that auxiliary variables such as object position, orientation, and size are communicated through recurrence and contribute significantly to performance improvement.  This evidence confirms our hypothesis that auxiliary variables are utilized to optimize object categorization in cluttered environments.  Notably, auxiliary variables were found to enhance performance in tasks involving non-rotation object categories, but not in tasks involving rotation-based categories, thereby indicating the dependence of recurrence on task type.  This research provides the first systematic explanation of how recurrence in recurrent neural networks contributes to improved object categorization performance.  Additionally, our findings offer a novel method of leveraging auxiliary variables, known perception metadata, to achieve superior object categorization in complex conditions.  This research has the potential to advance the development of object categorization systems, particularly those requiring robust performance in challenging environments.  This research could also inform the design of future object categorization systems capable of accurately identifying objects in real-world settings where variability in position, orientation, and size is inevitable. Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a significant unresolved issue. We conducted an in-depth analysis of correlated non-Hermitian systems, with a particular focus on the topological characteristics of one-dimensional systems. Our results reveal that correlations cause a significant reduction in the topological classification from $\mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ for one-dimensional systems with a single synthetic dimension, along with $\mathrm{U(1)}$ symmetry and spin-parity symmetry. We also investigated the properties of an extended Hatano-Nelson chain, which demonstrates substantial correlation effects; interactions abolish the skin effect that exists in the non-interacting system. The findings of this study underscore the instability of the skin effect against correlations, which is consistent with the reduced point-gap topology in one spatial dimension. The discoveries presented here provide novel insights into the topological characteristics of correlated systems, thereby initiating new areas of research within the field of non-Hermitian topological physics. The findings can be empirically demonstrated in systems such as superconducting quantum billiards that incorporate Rashba layers in semiconductor nanowires or synthetic quantum systems designed with encircling atomic or Rydberg atoms. The generation of robust momentum-correlated entanglement through topological edge states, along with the production of image states at exceptional points after interaction, also emerge as feasible possibilities; these could serve as the foundation for the development of novel correlation-based technologies, potentially including quantum information technologies and specialized quantum batteries. The reduced point-gap topology in one spatial dimension can be represented by a single real number; this realization further contributes to the comprehensive classification of correlated systems in one spatial dimension, which remains an open challenge. The reductions seen here include the loss of skinness and the reduction of $\mathrm{U(1)}$ charge for systems with synthetic dimensions; these discoveries indicate that correlations can either eliminate or modify the topological characteristics of systems with synthetic dimensions, thereby rendering them unsuitable for topology-based device design. The findings of this study also emphasize the instability of the pseudospin polarization that commonly exists in systems with synthetic dimensions due to interactions with correlations. The reductions seen here also underscore the distinct characteristics of systems with genuine two-dimensional systems, which are capable of supporting multiple topological invariants despite the influence of correlations. Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is established to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad. Our findings demonstrate that GCM arrays can be generated for any size of n, with precoding employing these arrays ensuring the maintenance of the maximum minimum distance between points in a lattice, even after encoding. Importantly, the novel constructions we've developed can serve as the fundamental building blocks for larger GCM structures, potentially extending to spaces of higher dimensions. The research presents four-dimensional GCM arrays as an example, which can be extended to five-dimensional GCM arrays, thereby opening the door for future research into higher-dimensional structures. The proposed GCM constructions also provide insights into the theoretical upper limits on the size of GCM arrays. The ideas presented in this research may be extended to construct higher-dimensional Golay complementary arrays, potentially encompassing spaces of five or more dimensions. The novel GCM structures we've developed could also find practical applications in various areas, such as differential geometry, algebraic geometry, curve fitting, and the design of spatial modulation communication systems. The integration of GCM arrays in these fields may provide enhanced performance through the preservation of key properties. The specific details we've presented could also be useful in the study of linear codes with unique weight profiles. The connections between our findings and linear code research are yet to be fully explored. The potential links between linear code studies and GCM constructions could yield cross-disciplinary innovations. The research provides a foundation for future studies, which could further establish the relationships between GCM arrays and linear codes. The theoretical upper limits on the size of GCM arrays, as presented by our findings, may also find applications in the design of Golay codes. The novel GCM constructions we've developed could provide an alternative perspective for understanding the size constraints of Golay codes. The ideas we've presented could lead to novel approaches in coding theory and spatial modulation design.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, molecular orientation, spin alignment, and quantum valley degeneracy which are often overlooked.
To investigate the distinct influences of these factors, we have developed a method to control and align the valley, spin, and charge states of phosphorus dopants in silicon.
Our results demonstrate the emergence of interference patterns in the probability distribution of electrons around the dopants, reveal exchange interactions sensitive to the orientation of valence orbitals, and expose the distinction in tunneling probabilities of electrons occupying different orbital valleys.
This study empowers the manipulation of electron behavior based on valley and spin characteristics, thus opening the door for the utilization of quantum tunneling as a tool to manage and direct electron interactions in solid-state quantum technologies. Ultimately, this research may pave the way for the development of valley-based quantum processors. Given that valley effects are confined to two-dimensional systems, silicon's bulk nature, featuring multiple valley degeneracies, presents an opportunity to explore collective behavior of valley-based entanglements on a larger scale. Additionally, controlling the spin and valley alignment of coupled dopants could give rise to distinct forms of entanglement that can be harnessed for information storage in solid-state quantum systems. Given the widespread application of silicon as a semiconductor in modern electronics, this research may have far-reaching implications for the optimization and enhancement of electronic transport within solid-state devices. Ultimately, this study may provide a foundation for the development of valley-based quantum processors and serve as a starting point for investigating collective valley effects in quantum systems. Given the distinct forms of tunneling interactions encountered here, we propose that valley effects, evident in the interference patterns and correlated states of dopant spins, could be leveraged to increase the efficiency of electronic transport in silicon by aligning valence orbits and reducing electron interaction based on valley degeneracy. Additionally, our results may provide a starting point for the optimization and enhancement of electronic transport in silicon-based devices by controlling the valley-based interaction between electrons. Given the notable contrast between Heisenberg and Coulomb interactions observed here, we anticipate that our findings will inspire the development of novel methods for reducing electron interactions and increasing the efficiency of electronic transport in silicon. Several disciplines have been influenced by optimization techniques that
can handle numerous scenarios effectively, leading to a growing need for
experts in optimization engineering. We create software solutions to address
this demand, as developing these tools from scratch is often time-consuming and
requires specialized knowledge. We introduce LibOPT, a versatile and open-source
framework for efficiently implementing various optimization strategies. It
features a user-friendly, prototyping-oriented approach and provides multiple
pre-built algorithms and versatile solution evaluation objects. We showcase
five different optimization scenarios that can be solved using LibOPT, taking
less time to develop than traditional methods. LibOPT is primarily designed to
be user-friendly and easily customizable, allowing experts to create their own
applications quickly. We outline the general architecture of an OPT application
and provide a comprehensive guide on how to extend and modify LibOPT to tackle
specific problems. Additionally, LibOPT comes with a comprehensive set of
features and optimization algorithms that can be used to develop new applications
efficiently. We use a reverse engineering approach to identify common patterns
and opportunities for reusing existing code within the library. This leads to a
faster development process and higher quality software by facilitating the
creation of new optimization algorithms. We compare LibOPT to other available
platforms and highlight its unique features, such as its focus on solving specific
problems and its prototyping-oriented approach, which differs from other more
general and theoretically-focused optimization libraries. Finally, LibOPT is
now available under the permissive APACHE 2.0 license, allowing developers to
use and modify the library to address their specific optimization challenges. We
invite experts in optimization to collaborate with us in making LibOPT a
leading open-source framework for tackling a wide range of practical optimization
problems. This collaborative effort can result in a plethora of new optimization
algorithms, significantly advancing the field and translating theoretical concepts
into robust and practical software solutions. You can visit our website at

Given an algebraic variety X that has a transitive action from the group Aut(X), the highest degree of transitivity of this action is called the transitivity degree. This degree is denoted by the maximum value of m for which Aut(X) acts transitively m times on X. In cases where Aut(X) is m-transitive for any positive value of m, we define the transitivity degree to be infinite. This study involves determining the transitivity degree for specific varieties, such as quasi-affine toric varieties, and homogeneous spaces, while exploring related open problems and conjectures. To accomplish this, we examined the sequence of degrees associated with the action of Aut(X) on its orbit-stabilizer variety, constructed by W. Klein. By analyzing this sequence, we determined the transitivity degree for specific varieties, such as projective space and its Grassmann variety. Additionally, we found that deg(X) is a geometrically invariant characteristic of the variety X. To do this, we considered non-degenerate projective varieties and defined the degree of an algebraic group action, establishing relationships between this degree and topological invariants. Finally, we investigated the transitivity degree of compact homogeneous spaces, such as flag varieties and projective spaces, while examining an open problem related to deg(G/S), the degree of the action of a group G on a variety S. This study attempts to clarify a significant result from J. Wolfram's research and proposes an alternative definition for the degree of an algebraic group action based on a different method of determining G/S degrees. Ultimately, we explored connections between the transitivity degree and other geometric characteristics of algebraic varieties, such as the Chow ring's characteristic degree. As a result, this study may contribute to the development of new methods for computing transitivity degrees, expanding upon existing techniques from differential geometry and algebraic geometry. In particular, we examined relationships between the transitivity degree and integral Chow forms, expressing deg(X) as a sum of characteristic Chow forms for specific homogeneous varieties. This investigation may lead to novel applications of Chow forms in describing algebraic varieties, such that deg(X) can be computed from just the Chow ring of X. To accomplish this, we analyzed Chern classes and other cohomology classes of algebraic varieties, exploring their relationships to the transitivity degree and geometric characteristics of the variety X. We apply the two-photon absorption transient current technique to study
properties of wide bandgap semiconductors. We utilize this technique to
investigate charge transport in scCVD diamond by exciting its charge carriers
with a femtosecond laser. Due to its two-photon nature, the technique confines
charge carrier generation in 3-D around the laser focal point. This localized
charge injection enables us to study the semiconductor bulk with high 3-D
resolution. We mapped the diamond's bulk electrical field at varying depths by
taking advantage of charge spatial confinement. The results were then compared
to X-ray diffraction topography. The approach allows for unique insights into
spatial charge transport variations in transparent wide bandgap materials.

Social media platforms are facing significant problems due to the presence of toxic content like hate speech, off-color language, and misogyny. These difficulties have caught the attention of the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community, driving innovative research in the field. In this study, we report on the performance of our models in the inaugural Arabic Misogyny Identification challenge, where we evaluate three models that can learn multiple tasks simultaneously, alongside their individual-task counterparts. Our approach relies on the use of Misogyny Identification datasets, consisting of annotated data and raw social media content, to inform our models' training. Our results indicate that the proposed models achieve high levels of accuracy across various evaluation metrics, indicating the potential for future research in this area. Additionally, we provide an in-depth analysis of our models' performance in the context of the unique linguistic and cultural characteristics of Arabic. Our code and datasets are publicly accessible for reproduction and further investigation. In a notable contribution, we achieve top-ranked results in the mistasked-AR category, where our primary model is designed to recognize misogynic text in the context of hate speech. Our secondary model, however, demonstrates top-performances in the individual tasks of misogynic text identification and categorization. Our success in this research underscores the effectiveness of multi-task learning in the identification and categorization of misogynic content, where fine-tuning pre-trained models on data-specific objectives can yield outstanding results, especially when data is scarce. Our exploration also sheds light on the challenges posed by text classification in the presence of data-class imbalance, alongside the complexities arising from distinct data sources with disparate linguistic and cultural characteristics. In the end, our investigation highlights the significance of thorough data evaluation for the development of reliable NLP models, specifically when processing sensitive topics like misogyny, where context is essential. Our model is subsequently adapted to recognize hate speech in Arabic, an area where research is currently underrepresented. Several key network communication challenges such as caching and computation are interconnected. A centralized caching approach seeks to mitigate network strain during peak wireless network times, whereas distributed computation explores the balance between computation and communication within a distributed system. This paper, drawing inspiration from a study of arithmetic sequences, introduces a comprehensive framework for creating caching schemes. This framework enables connections between caching schemes and numerous combinatorial objects, offering versatility in scheme design. We show that schemes built using a placement delivery array can be expressed through a new approach, and other known schemes can also be accommodated within this framework. Furthermore, we use this framework to develop new caching schemes with reduced communication costs for arbitrary arithmetic sequences with specific properties. We also extend this framework to apply to distributed computation schemes, offering a novel method for calculating lower bounds on data transfer within a computation network. We verify the efficiency of this framework through applications to specific scenarios. Our results demonstrate the potential for enhancing existing caching and computation schemes by re-examining their underlying structures. We also observe that the introduced framework is applicable to a broader range of schemes, offering opportunities for new discoveries. A related resource is available online in a MATLAB file. Natural language processing, a crucial field of study, strives to comprehend text via digital analysis, despite the inherent imperfections arising from diverse forms of written and spoken language. This work delves into employing various graph-based methodologies for resolving the challenge of text summarization via a selective extraction technique. Two key indicators – sentence overlap and edit distance – are employed for gauging sentence similarity. Additionally, the research assesses multiple sentence similarity measurement approaches, including Jaccard, Levenshtein, and Cosine similarity, across four summarization datasets. Our study finds that the Jaccard approach yields the most optimal results across all datasets, achieving success rates of 92.5%, 91.2%, 90.5%, and 89.3%. Furthermore, we introduce a novel graph-based text summarization framework that builds upon the Jaccard similarity measure and utilizes a threshold of 0.2 to isolate unique sentences for summarization. This framework is compared to the leading Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) approaches. Our analysis indicates that the proposed method surpasses LSA and LDA in 7 out of 8 summarization datasets, achieving superior results. The integration of Cosine similarity into the graph-based approach enhances its performance, yielding improved outcomes in 5 out of 8 summarization datasets. Our study showcases the efficacy of graph-based methodologies combined with diverse similarity measures for text summarization. The proposed graph-based approach is anticipated to serve as a reliable solution for resolving the challenge of text summarization. The source code used in this research is publicly accessible via GitHub. Furthermore, the generated summaries and evaluation results are publicly available via a created website. Two summarization datasets were employed, comprising news articles and questions, while a third dataset consisted of emails. Our study examines the feasibility of graph-based methodologies in natural language processing, highlighting their potential to address complex text-based challenges. The integration of graph-based approaches could potentially expedite the development of effective natural language processing solutions, thereby enhancing their performance to a notable extent. The proposed graph-based approach is anticipated to contribute positively to the advancement of computer science. Its potential applications are diverse, encompassing areas such as search engine optimization, content creation, and question answering, where summarizing content based on similarity can yield improved results. In particular, graph-based methodologies may lead to more targeted and relevant content recommendations. The proposed graph-based approach is set to undergo testing in content creation scenarios, where its unique mechanism is expected to yield superior outcomes.

Polynomial system solving plays a crucial role in various applications to capture nonlinear geometric attributes. To obtain a solution set devoid of degeneration, which end-users seek to avoid, the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system needs to be computed. The nondegenerate locus comprises points where the codimension of the solution set matches the number of equations in the system. Historically, the nondegenerate locus has been obtained using ideal-theoretic techniques in conjunction with signature-based algorithms like Groebner basis computation and Buchberger's algorithm modified for nondegenerate solutions. Building upon these algorithms, a novel signature-based algorithm is introduced to directly calculate the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system through nonnormality signatures without requiring intermediate intermediate ideals, thus streamlining the process and eliminating unnecessary steps. The algorithm's first-generation variant is described, along with enhancements to their second-generation variants that incorporate signature transformation andmsolve. The feasibility and efficiency of the proposed algorithm are validated by means of numerical experiments. By calculating the $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess in the $e^{+}e^{-}$ mass distribution over hadronic contributions, we found that quasi-real direct virtual photons significantly contribute to the photon spectrum. In Cu$+$Cu collisions, photons show a clear increase above a binary-scaled $p$$+$$p$ fit, and their transverse momentum spectra follow a similar trend as Au$+$Au collisions, involving a similar number of participants. The Turan tetrahedron problem seeks to calculate the Turan density of the tetrahedron graph K4^3 by finding the maximum l1-norm of a K4^3-free n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraph's codegree vector. We develop a new method for determining hypergraph extremality and apply it to calculate the asymptotic extremal function of the tetrahedron graph under our novel framework. The codegree squared sum, or co2(G), is introduced to measure codegree magnitude in a 3-uniform hypergraph, with exco2(n,H) representing the maximal codegree squared sum among n-vertex H-free hypergraphs. Utilizing flag algebra computations, we determine the codegree squared extremal numbers for K4^3 and K5^3 and demonstrate associated stability properties, revealing the structural resemblance of extremal K4^3-free hypergraphs to the conjectured extremal hypergraphs of Turan's tetrahedron problem. Additionally, we identify key general characteristics of exco2(n,H), such as the existence of a scaled limit and invariance under vertex blow-up. These findings are pivotal to our algorithmic approach, which relies on a ground-up strategy and an iterative process driven by difference methods. The extremal hypergraphs obtained through our method have recently been proven nearly optimal for the tetrahedron problem under our l1-norm framework. However, it remains unknown whether these limits apply to the traditional L1-norm, with the potential existence of a gap. Nevertheless, our findings represent the first accurate calculation of asymptotic extremal values for the tetrahedron problem, achieving a 1-o(1) error rate. Consequently, we derive a precise estimate for the tetrahedron problem's asymptotic extremal value: the limit of the tetrahedron problem's critical value l1(H4(n)) as n approaches infinity is 1/2. This result is inherently significant, as it presents an alternative approach for distinguishing hypergraph extremality based on codegree magnitude measurements. The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that the modified operator converges to the original function at a rate of $h^2$ as the mesh size $h$ approaches zero. In addition to theoretical analysis, we examine the method's performance through a range of numerical experiments. The results indicate that the adapted operator converges at a rate of $h^2$ and preserves both monotonicity and convexity even in the presence of noisy data. It outperforms a comparable method constructed using Gaussian RBF while requiring fewer computations. The proposed interpolation operator is primarily designed for applications involving function values but can also effectively handle linear gradients. Pulsar halos are diffuse, high-energy emitters originating from ancient pulsar wind nebulae, characterized by thin, extended gamma-ray emission. Research has focused on two distinct types of halos: those surrounding pulsars still emitting gamma-rays and those no longer emitting gamma-rays. Studies of the former have investigated the long-term pulsar wind nebulosity, whereas analyses of the latter have explored the prolonged evolution of pulsar wind nebulae. Investigations of halo gamma-ray emission have led to discoveries of new pulsars and nebulae, and assessments of potential very-high-energy emission from halos are also being conducted. This review examines halo characteristics, formation mechanisms, and emission phenomena, as well as their use in understanding pulsar and nebula evolution, using data from the Lambda-CDM model for galaxy structure and formation, and incorporating realistic predictions for star formation and supernovae. Finally, studies of halo gamma rays have implications for our understanding of pulsar magnetic field decay and star formation histories in the galaxy. In the future, studies of halo gamma rays from the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope will continue to shed light on these topics, particularly by expanding our knowledge of halo gamma-ray emission to higher energies. For instance, it is likely that a substantial portion of halo emission will be attributed to leptonic scattering, rather than more complex emission mechanisms. Moreover, a comprehensive understanding of halo emission from pulsar wind nebulae using data from the Fermi All-sky Survey will facilitate precision comparisons with simulations of galaxy structure and formation. This will ultimately enable gamma-ray studies of halo emission to serve as a unique probe of galaxy structure and formation. As a result, a deeper understanding of halo gamma-ray emission from pulsar wind nebulae is crucial for unraveling the complex and diverse nature of pulsar star formation and supernovae in the galaxy. Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which encompasses nine distinct weather categories and is designed for use in European climates.
Additionally, we develop an image augmentation technique tailored to recognizing weather conditions based on the RFS labels.
Our evaluations involve comparing the performance of several Convolutional Neural Network configurations, utilizing the RFS dataset, to determine the most effective weather condition classification method.
Our research establishes a new benchmark for weather classification and identifies the optimal network architecture for this specific task. Our work also highlights the challenges of detecting the 'clear' weather condition, suggesting that further research is necessary to overcome these difficulties. Our source code and dataset are publicly accessible on GitHub. Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility, yet accurately modeling and controlling them to grasp objects efficiently remains challenging. Soft grippers' infinite-dimensionality and non-linearity make traditional control approaches difficult to implement. In response, researchers have turned to data-driven methods. However, current methods typically require extensive model learning through simulations or offline processes, which often fails to adapt to novel scenarios or dynamic environmental changes. In this research, we present an innovative online algorithm that uses the Koopman operator theory to update a dynamic model in real-time, effectively accounting for variations in dimensionality and non-linearity. To ensure smooth model adaptation, our algorithm also incorporates a model-predictive control strategy, providing optimal control inputs to achieve desired outcomes. We demonstrate the efficacy of our algorithm using a soft multi-fingered gripper in a robotic hand, successfully grasping various shapes and adapting to unexpected changes in soft material properties. The integration of this online algorithm enables true learning and adaptation at runtime, empowering robots to adapt to unforeseen circumstances and learn from their experiences. The research presents a novel solution to the long-standing problem of modeling and adapting to soft dynamics in robots. The novel algorithm was successfully validated in experiments and outperformed previous results in multiple indices. The research resulted in two significant contributions: (i) the development of an online dynamic model for high-dimensional non-linear systems using the Koopman operator theory, and (ii) the integration of the model with model-predictive control, enabling adaptive control in real-world scenarios. The research was conducted using a sophisticated setup, including a 3D printing and an optical sensing system that allowed the deployment of the algorithm in a multi-fingered gripper. One of the fundamental problems in science and engineering involves finding the lowest cost value for a given function, known as an optimization problem. Various numerical methods have been proposed to solve this problem, but the Gradient Descent method remains the most popular due to its ease and effectiveness. Nonetheless, this approach faces challenges with local minima and slow convergence, particularly when near the optimal point. In response, researchers developed the Natural Gradient Descent method to improve performance across multiple domains, including machine learning, tensor networks, and quantum algorithms. Our work presents a new method to further expand upon NGD, utilizing a suitable reference manifold to expedite convergence and enhance understanding of optimization methods. We demonstrate a general approach to selecting the reference manifold, allowing for integration of prior knowledge about the function. Our proposal is illustrated through successful applications in simple cost functions and the training of a fully connected neural network. Additionally, our method offers enhanced transparency and interpretability of the optimization process. We anticipate that our work will contribute to the development of more effective optimization methods, informed by a deeper understanding of the underlying cost functions. High-energy emissions from ancient supermassive black holes can provide a direct look into the black hole activity in the early universe. Specifically, misaligned jets of high-redshift active galaxies should make up a significant portion of these distant galaxy populations. This study uses data collected from observations of a distant galaxy called J2102+6015, a compact radio source located 10 billion light-years away. Its spectral energy distribution, characterized by a steep energy decline, is similar to that of another ancient galaxy called 0725-668. Analyzing its spectral properties yields evidence of a compact object releasing energy in the X-ray band, likely a supermassive black hole. Its radio and X-ray emissions are linked through the inverse Compton process, driven by highly energetic electrons. Jet alignment was also investigated using observations of its polarized emission in the radio band, but the data didn't provide clear evidence of aligned jets. J2102+6015 exhibits characteristics of an extremely young and highly energetic active galaxy, one of the youngest of its kind. Its massive black hole, however, is remarkably less massive than what's typically expected. Its substantial black hole mass, however, does support the idea that massive black holes were present in the early universe, even if they weren't yet part of massive galaxy systems. Its massive black hole likely caused the surrounding gas cloud to collapse, initiating both the black hole growth and massive galaxy development. This process, known as a self-regulated feedback loop, should have been active in the early universe, one powered by repeated active black hole outbursts. This likely set the stage for how galaxy properties were shaped and preserved. Its distant counterpart, 0725-668, also displays similar characteristics. This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective solutions. Current methods, both traditional and deep learning-based, primarily rely on single-textual sources such as patient demographics and clinical history. Unlike existing approaches, this study explores the potential of combining multiple data types like text-based clinical information and visual medical scans to inform survival time predictions, thereby enhancing accuracy and learning patterns. Notably, this work introduces the first instance of using radiological data for survival forecasting. Experimental results on a large lung cancer dataset confirm that incorporating multiple data types of high-quality medical information yields significantly better predictions than models utilizing individual data types or simpler models. Additionally, this study performs comprehensive analyses on the relative impact of each medical information type and verifies the model's performance using independent test sets. To evaluate the model's predictive accuracy, mean absolute error and grid-based brier score metrics are employed. Importantly, this research is the first to apply deep learning-based methods to predict lung cancer survival times using medical imaging. These findings have the potential to advance survival time forecasting using a diverse range of high-quality medical information, ultimately contributing to more precise and individualized prognosis for lung cancer patients. A well-designed state representation is crucial in the learning process of Reinforcement Learning. Natural language can be utilized in numerous tasks to either represent the state or constitute it entirely. This overview focuses on the techniques employed by researchers to create natural language state representations, underscoring the need for more transparent and contextualized models, thorough justification of design choices and assessments of the relative effectiveness of varying methodologies. We examine key challenges and opportunities related to the use of natural language in state representation, and consider several control-related issues such as confidence estimation and dataset partitioning. We distinguish between two primary approaches: one that views language as a means to represent the state and another where the entire state is comprised of language. We examine existing solutions to three categories of tasks: predictive modeling, optimization and control. This survey seeks to provide a comprehensive understanding of the range of techniques employed to formulate natural language state representations and highlight open research problems. This paper examines certain types of non-weight modules connected to Lie algebras of the Weyl type. Firstly, we establish the characteristics of modules whose restrictions to $U(\frak h)$ are one-dimensional over Lie algebras representing differential operators on a circle. We then identify the requirements for the irreducibility of tensor products between quasi-finite highest weight modules and modules free over $U(\frak h)$. Additionally, we show that these tensor products are isomorphic only if their corresponding base modules are equivalent, before expanding our findings to cover general Lie algebras representing differential operators. Finally, we identify the characteristics of modules whose restrictions to $U(\frak h)$ are one-dimensional in the context of soliton-free highest weight modules and demonstrate that these constraints apply to the entire algebra. Our investigation also reveals the connection between the characteristics of modules free over $U(\frak h)$ and the branching rules for representation branching from the tensor product of two irreducible highest weight modules. This analysis represents a significant extension of the theorem on the restriction of tensor products to weight modules, originally proved by the co-authors, to cover the scenario in which the first tensor factor is not a highest weight module. As a result, our study generalizes the theorem to cover the scenario in which the first tensor factor is a module free over $U(\frak h)$. Furthermore, our investigation establishes the theorem on the restriction of tensor products to cover the scenario in which the second tensor factor is a module free over $U(\frak h)$ and reveals the characteristics of modules satisfying the conditions for the irreducibility of tensor products between highest weight modules and modules free over $U(\frak h)$. This analysis represents a significant extension of the investigation on the soliton-free conditions for representation branching, originally carried out by the co-authors. As a result, our study generalizes the investigation to cover the scenario in which the first tensor factor is a highest weight module and reveals the characteristics of modules free over $U(\frak h)$. We expect that our findings will also be applicable to other Lie algebras representing differential operators. Consequently, our examination of the properties of modules connected to the Lie algebra $sl_3(\mathcal D)$ will serve as a practical demonstration of the transferability of our findings to other Lie algebras representing differential operators. Recent advances in open-domain dialogue systems have achieved significant breakthroughs, but developing a robust dialogue system tailored to a specific role remains a challenging task. To tackle this issue, we introduce a novel framework comprising two primary modules: a role assessment module and a dialogue management module. The role assessment module evaluates candidate responses to determine the suitability of roles and assigns a priority level to the selected response. The dialogue management module integrates user inputs to produce a response that meets role requirements. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework by integrating it with a large-language model conversational interface, achieving notable results on the SemEval 2017 RoleCon dataset. Moreover, we showcase the potential of our model to support multiple roles and adapt to data augmentation and language model pre-training. The source code of our model is freely accessible on GitHub.

Unlike the more common gravitational wave background produced by binary black holes, SGWMB's characteristics remain relatively unchanged when the detector's angular resolution is considered. Therefore, resolving SGWMB likely requires high-frequency, low-frequency or broadband observations with large detectors. This semantic communication system utilizes a neural network-based language model, which dynamically generates vocabulary based on context-specific noise. As a result, data transmission is optimized, and the need for high data rate transmission is eliminated. Furthermore, the system's reliability is further enhanced by the system's ability to mitigate the adverse effects of noise through iterative message recovery. The Natural Language Processing area has garnered disproportionate interest from researchers in the past. A primary factor driving this attention lies in the word prediction challenge, where given a sequence of words in a sentence, a model is tasked with recommending the subsequent word. Researchers have addressed this issue through various techniques, combining either syntactic or semantic analysis methods in the past. However, individually, these approaches often fail to yield practical results in real-world applications. For instance, latent semantic analysis can capture semantic text characteristics, yet it disregards syntactic constraints when generating word suggestions. In contrast, more advanced models like Deep Learning integrate both methods to achieve impressive outcomes. While these models can handle complex natural language phenomena, they typically demand sizeable datasets, rendering them impractical for newly crafted sentences and limited-domain scenarios. In response to these limitations, this research presents a hybrid model that merges the Naive Bayes and latent semantic analysis methodologies to forecast word choices in a sentence. The proposed system evaluates sentence grammaticality and relevance before selecting words that align with both its structural and semantic properties. The model's effectiveness is validated through experiments conducted on two datasets consisting of incorrect and semantically inconsistent sentences. The evaluation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms baseline systems consisting of either Naive Bayes or latent semantic analysis in both test sets. Moreover, the results showcase the proposed model's capability to make accurate word predictions in sentence contexts. Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to provide accurate, reliable information to users worldwide, but its vast knowledge base is threatened by an overwhelming volume of low-quality content pages. The problem stems from Wikipedia's open-editing policy, allowing anyone to modify articles, including inaccuracies. To address this issue, we developed a system that flags potential weaknesses in Wikipedia articles, indicating the need for review by the community. By analyzing editor behaviors and patterns related to specific categories, our system identifies articles at risk of suffering from low-quality content. Using natural language processing and machine learning, we labeled articles based on patterns found in Wikipedia's metadata, ultimately presenting a key contribution towards solving the open problem of automatically labeling low-quality content on Wikipedia. Experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of our proposed method in identifying article problems and labeling them with relevant categories. The effectiveness of our approach is further validated by showing that editing behaviors can be harnessed to achieve results comparable to methods that examine article text. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. This proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd. Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.3±0.2±0.4) ×10^-4, with the given uncertainties stemming from various sources. The relative ratio of the $B^0_s$ decay modes to neutral $B$ mesons is found to be 0.237±0.009±0.003, which is consistent with the standard model predictions at the time of the study's completion. Furthermore, a search for left-handed $W$-electron coupling by examining lepton flavor universality in the $\bar{D}^0\mu^-\gamma$ decay mode at high $q^2$ did not yield notable evidence. Instead, a modification in the $R_D$ ratio, which compares the decay modes of $B$ mesons to muons and electrons, did not reveal any notable deviations within the examined range of $q^2$. The study does, however, set an upper limit on possible violations of this ratio due to new physics at 5.1(4.9) ×10^-3, which corresponds to 3.0 (2.9) TeV, at 95% confidence level. The data collected also enabled the determination of the $B^0_s$ decay length, which was found to be 0.514±0.017 ps. The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, isospectral pairs of manifolds, and other examples. Building upon an established method, we derive new T-duals from a variety of isospectral pairs, including torus bundles, isospectral pairs of Grassmannians, and other manifolds. In addition, we examine the properties of the dual algebra and show that for many cases, the dualizing functors can be represented as Banach $C^*$-algebra homomorphisms. It is also demonstrated that the application of topological T-duality can be effectively utilized to identify universal Chern-Connes morphisms and universal duals. Ultimately, we illustrate that topological T-duality offers a versatile framework for identifying universal duals through a combination of mathematical concepts and techniques. This approach is shown to be versatile and effective in a wide range of situations. Additionally, we were unable to conclusively determine whether the Banach $C^*$-algebra duals we constructed are actual $C^*$-algebras of spaces. This indicates that topological T-duality can be a valuable tool for exploring novel perspectives on isospectral pairs of spaces. In particular, we found that topological T-duality provides a method for identifying universal Chern-Connes morphisms and universal duals, which is a key aspect in noncommutative geometry. This development is an expansion of our understanding of the relationship between space, duality, and algebra. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents competitively. The performing agent' actions are then transferred to the observing agent, which imitates the former's policies using behavior cloning. The novelty lies in replacing traditional expert demonstrations with competitor-derived experiences, thus eliminating the need for extensive expertise collection. Moreover, peer-agent experiences are inherently diverse, decreasing data requirements for imitation learning. Our experimental results demonstrate improved efficiency and optimal policy convergence using this method. The approach has potential applications in scenarios where peer-agent interaction is feasible and expert guidance is financially prohibitive. This paper proposes a metric function that yields an efficient decoding strategy for programmable-accuracy convolutional (PAC) codes. We develop a formula to calculate code density, enabling the construction of PAC codes with specified parameters, including rate, depth, error probability, and redundancy. We also establish a method for determining the minimum number of transmissions required to achieve a specified error probability in PAC codes. Our studies demonstrate that, under certain conditions, PAC codes can offer improved transmission efficiency relative to low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. Furthermore, our work enables the development of PAC code ensembles with programmable error probabilities and variable rates. We illustrate the effectiveness of our proposals through numerical examinations of PAC code performance in diverse scenarios. Our findings indicate that PAC codes can enhance decoder accuracy and reduce transmission latency relative to LDPC codes in systems requiring low error rates. Conversely, LDPC codes generally exhibit superior performance in scenarios where latency is a minor concern. We provide further insights into PAC code performance via investigations of binary PAC code ensembles. These investigations reveal non-inflection points in the union of pairwise weights' cumulative distribution functions, which dictate the efficacy of various decoding strategies. We demonstrate the existence of a threshold in the relative error probability in binary PAC codes, necessitating further research into PAC code properties beyond this threshold. We also show that enhancing the error probability in binary PAC codes typically reduces their transmission latency and accelerates decoding. We validate our theoretical analyses through simulations, confirming our predictions and offering practical recommendations for PAC code design. Furthermore, our work in this paper lays a foundational understanding of binary PAC code behavior, which will guide the development of novel coding strategies. We incorporate error exponential weights into binary PAC codes to exhibit distinct behavior, expand the scope of our studies to include binary PAC code ensembles, and offer potential directions for exploring the theoretical limits of PAC codes. We also compare the performance of binary PAC codes with LDPC codes, illustrating their varying applicability in different scenarios. We strive to make our contributions more transparent by presenting our investigations in an approachable manner and offering plain-English interpretations of our results. Additionally, we verify the correctness of our theoretical analyses through simulations, offering a concise summary of our studies and the associated code. We make frequent references to our accompanying code, which substantiates our theoretical findings and facilitates the replication of our research. We also offer generalizations of our contributions, applying the metrics and algorithms we've developed to diverse coding theories and scenarios. We make our accompanying code available at https://github.com/felipeoupa/pac

This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud data, starting from the known poses in the initial frame. To achieve this, we introduce a network called HandTrackNet, the first point cloud-based hand joint tracking system, which uses a two-stage process. The first stage, an encoder-decoder module, predicts potential hand joint movements between frames and reconstructs the new hand joint configurations, while the second stage, a tracker, uses a novel sequence-based association metric to match these predicted movements with the actual changes and track the hand and objects in a sequence. To evaluate HandTrackNet, we created a new and extensive dataset called HOHI, which contains 105 real-world video streams with diverse hand and object interactions. The results show that HandTrackNet outperforms current state-of-the-art hand pose estimation and tracking methods on HOHI. Moreover, we analyzed HandTrackNet's robustness by visualizing its performance on various challenging scenarios derived from HOHI. To ensure trustworthiness, we also conducted ablation studies and case studies that examine how changes in HandTrackNet's design affect its performance. The code and HOHI dataset are open-source and available for public use. The reconstruction of the dataset, which requires significant human annotation, was made possible through a collaborative effort with MTech, a leading AI training and data annotation service. The HOHI dataset can now be used by the AI community as a valuable resource for developing new and advanced hand and object interaction tracking methods. To validate the accuracy of HandTrackNet's and the HOHI dataset, we created new state-of-the-art depth-based hand and object pose estimation and tracking methods that serve as gold standards. These new methods, which are referred to as DeepHandEst, were trained and evaluated on newly created datasets and sequences that are distinct from HOHI. The results show that HandTrackNet, which was initially trained on HOHI, achieves an error rate of 5.42 cm for tracking hands and objects in natural hand and object interactions, outperforming the current state-of-the-art tracking methods by a significant margin. In contrast, DeepHandEst, which was trained on newly created datasets and sequences, achieves even lower error rates of 4.81 cm. The success of these methods, which are based on the HOHI dataset and DeepHandEst's gold standard performances, mark a new milestone in the development of advanced hand and object interaction tracking and pose estimation methods. A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (focal units). We provide criteria to select these pivotal units under the given interference framework and conduct a simulation to assess existing methods for detecting interference in networks. By implementing this selection process, highly effective tests of treatment interference are achieved, surpassing the efficacy of standard experimental methods. This novel approach enables researchers to model and understand treatment interference within connected networks. Key words: treatment interference, neural networks, detection, CTT, f-regularity.

This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for the number of stabilizer states required to express $m$ copies of the magic state, $|T\rangle$. The findings reveal that a superposition of no more than $O(2^{\alpha m})$ stabilizer states can accurately represent $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$, where $\alpha\leq 0.3963$, surpassing the previous best-known estimate of $\alpha\leq 0.463$. This advancement allows for the development of a classical algorithm capable of approximating the output probabilities of $n$-qubit Clifford + T circuits $U$ within a specified inverse polynomial error margin, using a time complexity of $\mathrm{poly}(n,m)2^{\alpha m}$. Furthermore, the investigation yields refined bounds on the stabilizer rank of symmetric product states $|\psi\rangle^{\otimes m}$, ultimately leading to the creation of a strong simulation algorithm for circuits comprising Clifford gates and multiple instances of a fixed single-qubit Z gate, operating at a time complexity of $\text{poly}(n,m) m^{0.3963}$. An additional suggestion is presented for potentially enhancing the upper bounds through the design of specific linear codes. This work may also stimulate the exploration of potential connections between quantum circuits applying sequences of noisy Clifford and T gates and classical models utilizing random walks on weighted graphs. Leveraging quantum computing may enable resolving conjectures related to these complex graphs. Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra. The data showed a signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 50% of its spectra. This study reported the following-classification rates, which ranged from 50% to 80%, and a precise radial velocity measurement accuracy of 0.25-0.30 km/s. This paper details the survey's observational data and presents the first results, which involve double-lined spectroscopic binary systems, along with several other types of binary stars, and narrow absorption lines likely caused by foreground moving groups or common proper motion objects. It estimates that about 5.24% of the spectra belong to double-lined spectroscopic binary systems and around 9.91% to other binary stars. Additionally, further study is required to determine the potential second harvest area of the LAMOST-4 project. Finally, we outline our plans and prospects for future work, which include using the LAMOST-4 project to establish a database of ground-based spectroscopic data on the potential second harvest area of the Gaia mission. Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that utilizes a lowered supply voltage to minimize access time, thereby enabling high throughput, low latency, and adaptability to dense SRAM designs. In addition to these advantages, the proposed TRNG features a decreased energy consumption, randomized data patterns, and a enhanced entropy estimation, thus outperforming existing SRAM-based TRNGs in several areas. To validate the proposed design's reliability, simulations were conducted with real-world datasets. Furthermore, the statistical results of these experiments demonstrate the high quality of the generated random numbers. As such, the proposed TRNG can serve as a trustworthy source of randomness for numerous applications requiring high throughput, low latency, and dense SRAM integration. In order to facilitate understanding, the design files and simulation data for the proposed TRNG have been made available on an online public platform. In the future, the proposed TRNG can be implemented using standard CMOS technology and integrated into storage devices, cryptocurrency miners, and other systems for secure operation. Ultimately, the proposed TRNG design can serve as a scalable, efficient, and adaptable solution for generating high-quality random numbers in microelectronic systems. Specifically, it can generate 290 Mbits of random data per second while consuming only 0.073 pJ per bit at a 1.2 V voltage. This efficient paradigm has the potential to be incorporated into future randomized algorithms for computing where high throughput is a priority. In comparison to existing SRAM-based TRNGs, the proposed TuRaN boasts the highest throughput, lowest energy expenditure, fastest latency, and highest quality of generated random numbers. As such, it is an attractive option for securing random number generation in modern electronic systems. Specifically, it outperforms existing SRAM-based TRNGs by an average of 2.2 times in throughput, 3.6 times in energy efficiency, 2.5 times in latency, and 1.3 times in entropy quality. As such, the proposed TuRaN design can serve as a versatile and efficient solution for generating high-quality random numbers in electronic systems.

A preliminary design and simulation of a single-electron resistive switch has been developed, incorporating two linear molecules that interact electrostatically: one molecule is a single-electron transistor and the other is a single-electron trap. To confirm our design's validity, a theoretical analysis was performed using ab-initio electronic structure calculations and classical molecular dynamics. The results show that when a weak voltage is applied, the trap molecule captures an electron, and then the transistor molecule's conductivity increases due to increased charge carrier mobility. Following this, the trap releases the captured electron, resulting in a significant increase in the transistor's conductivity. This process can be repeated, allowing the system to transition between two stable states and exhibiting nonvolatile memory characteristics. Additionally, the simulations indicate that molecules with higher polarizability and higher lying LUMO energies tend to have higher switching thresholds. Conversely, molecules with higher lying HOMO energies tend to have lower switching thresholds. These findings enable the accurate selection of single-electron resistive switches from different classes of organic molecules. Furthermore, these devices offer the unique ability to simultaneously monitor and control the current flowing through the molecules, providing an innovative means of reliable and low-power monitoring of memory blocks. The system also exhibits resistance matching, meaning the same amount of current is required for both the set and reset processes. This resistance matching can be attributed to the system's tendency towards equilibrium, where the same charge mediates both processes. Consequently, the system's resistance does not change suddenly; rather, it gradually shifts between two stable states. Ultimately, the system's performance is largely determined by tuning the lead-molecule interaction and the charge density on the molecules. The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an attractive alternative to conventional methods. By applying loop-tree duality, the Feynman integrands are simplified to a form that only captures physical information, resulting in a causal representation. This enhanced integrand can then be evaluated using causal products, which are constructed from lower-loop and tree-level Feynman integrals. While the concept of causal products is theoretically sound, its practical implementation has been a limitation. In this study, we develop a crucial component required for the causal evaluation of Feynman integrals by introducing an innovative method for numerical causal products. By combining this result with the concept of loop-tree duality, we demonstrate a new technique for the causal evaluation of Feynman integrals. As a significant validation, we apply this method to evaluate the two-loop hexagon amplitude with full mass dependence in the limit of small QCD coupling. In this case, we also introduce an innovative approach for the numerical integration of Feynman integrals that reduces the complexity of loop-level causal components, resulting in a substantial performance enhancement. Specifically, we achieve a significant speedup of two orders of magnitude for the desired amplitude. Additionally, we verify that the results from our causal evaluation match the outcomes from standard methods within specified numerical errors. In a related development, we explore the concept of universal Feynman integrands, which are free from numerical factors, by combining loop-tree duality and the concept of master integrals. This leads to the discovery of a fundamental relationship between universal Feynman integrands and causal Feynman integrands. Furthermore, we embark on a detailed analysis of numerical issues that arise during the causal evaluation process, including non-zero integrals and numerical cancellations. Based on this understanding, we outline a strategy to address these numerical problems and showcase its effectiveness with several examples. Lastly, we examine the real-time behavior of universal Feynman integrands and reveal that their behavior is indeed causal, which is a necessary condition to represent universal Feynman integrands as causal products of lower-loop and tree-level Feynman integrals. This result has important implications for future research in this field. In another related development, we investigate the numerical evaluation of Feynman integrals using cutting-edge techniques from numerical integration and algebraic geometry. This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, similar to analogous methods used in the study of one-dimensional Schrödinger equations. A related theory involving the unitary evolution operator for quantum walks is also explored. As a result, we derive a formula that allows for the expression of any bounded function as a linear combination of the walk's eigenfunctions, given the operator's spectral properties. An associated representation theorem for bounded functions is then derived, followed by discussions on potential connections to harmonic analysis. Additionally, we examine properties of the walk's eigenfunctions, including periodic and decaying functions, and establish relationships to the walk's stationary states. Finally, we apply the derived theories to create a method for approximating certain types of integrable one-dimensional Schrödinger equations, specifically those defined through difference equations. This method relies on the convergence of specific bounded sequences related to the quantum walks. A relevant example is provided to illustrate the approach. We hope that this work will contribute to the development of a quantum analysis that is fundamentally distinct from traditional classical analysis. Our findings reveal that when thermal conduction is active, it prevents the formation of spiral structures, but when it's inhibited, small-density variations lead to spiral shape formations. Additionally, we discovered that when numerical methods are refined, cooling leads to cloud formations that grow over time. However, these structures tend to dissipate when magnetic fields are introduced, leading to a more uniform density distribution. Ultimately, our research indicates that cloud evolution is significantly impacted by a combination of factors, including magnetic fields, cooling rates, and thermal conduction. Although cloud evolution may not directly influence the overall galaxy cluster structure, it does play a vital role in understanding gas flow and energy dissipation within these systems. Notably, we found that when numerical methods are coarser, cooling leads to the formation of rings and bars, leading to reduced rates of star formation compared to more refined methods. Ultimately, our research suggests a decreased relationship between cooling rates and star formation rates, effectively resolving a longstanding, related inquiry in the field. To streamline this process, we've developed a multi-step optimization method, dividing the motion planning task into simpler sub-problems using data-driven modeling techniques to leverage problem structure and eliminate non-essential variables. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices. A key outcome of this research indicates that, for a certain range of parameters, solar radiation pressure can potentially stabilize low-altitude orbits that would otherwise be unstable in the absence of this perturbation. This finding holds true for orbital periods ranging from 100 to 450 minutes and semi-major axes between 1000 and 4500 kilometers. Overall, this research provides insight into the complex interactions between solar radiation pressure, orbital motion, and stability, offering valuable estimates and predictions for the performance and management of artificial satellites in orbit around the Earth. Furthermore, the techniques and models developed in this study can be adapted for application in space missions and the design of orbital control systems.
